response: The section details a systematic, reproducible workflow for building three literature corpora—main (RFM‑related, 81.2 %), implications (9.9 %), and further (8.9 %)—totaling 1,263 publications. It describes an automated acquisition pipeline, filtering and post‑processing steps, and the criteria governing each corpus’s composition and role in the review.

The authors built a fully automated, modular Python pipeline (Fig. 5) to retrieve and filter scholarly articles while limiting manual work to two “Manual Refinement” steps. Users supply one or more structured Academic Search Query Syntax (ASQS) queries, a date range, target databases (arXiv, Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scopus, Semantic Scholar), a retrieval preference (latest vs. most relevant), and per‑query caps (e.g., 100 results). The DB‑Search component translates each ASQS query into each database’s native syntax, relaxes unsupported operators, and runs all DB‑query permutations. Returned metadata are merged, duplicates removed via DOIs, and missing fields completed through auxiliary APIs (Semantic Scholar, arXiv, Crossref). Validity checks (e.g., title‑abstract consistency) discard malformed records, followed by a second duplicate pass. Results are saved as JSON/YAML (optionally PDF) with full citation details and auto‑generated reports of queries, timestamps, and counts per DB‑query pair. An on‑demand GPT‑4o filter scores semantic relevance, outputting binary labels, a 0‑1 score, and brief rationales; filters can be applied sequentially with stricter criteria. A separate GPT‑4o “Query Proposal” module suggests initial ASQS queries from user intent. After automated steps, the authors performed manual enrichment, correction, and additional filtering to ensure completeness and relevance, producing the final literature corpora used in the study.

Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) are presented as the robotic analogue of large‑scale foundation models in language and vision, distinguished by a “generalist core” that enables rapid adaptation across tasks, environments, and hardware with minimal engineering.  The authors argue that true RFMs must combine three capabilities: (1) multi‑modality, ingesting proprioceptive signals, images, and natural‑language instructions; (2) output flexibility, producing actions, plans, trajectories, or other control signals suitable for diverse robots; and (3) adaptability, allowing cross‑task or cross‑embodiment generalisation through high‑level prompts, goal images, demonstrations, or lightweight fine‑tuning.  They differentiate single‑purpose RFMs (focused on perception, planning, or control alone) from general‑purpose RFMs that integrate perception with actionable outputs, and they treat Vision‑Language‑Action models (VLAs) as a distinct sub‑category that satisfies the RFM criteria by aligning vision, language, and action into a common token format for end‑to‑end training.  Taxonomically, RFMs are grouped into (i) control‑oriented models that emit low‑level motor commands, (ii) planning‑oriented models that generate high‑level task decompositions or sub‑goals, and (iii) integrated models that jointly plan and control, representing the most ambitious step toward general robotic intelligence.  The survey notes that many existing approaches—e.g., vision‑action models without language, or domain‑specific manipulators—can still qualify as RFMs if they retain multi‑purpose adaptability.  Ultimately, a model is classified as an RFM only when it demonstrably transcends narrow, hardware‑specific solutions, offering cross‑task, cross‑embodiment flexibility while handling heterogeneous sensory inputs and producing versatile outputs.

The introduction frames industrial robotics as shifting from tightly engineered, static automation toward flexible, collaborative systems, especially cobots that must be commissioned quickly, redeployed across changing processes, and operate safely near humans. While mechanical performance is adequate, the bottleneck lies in robust, adaptive, and intuitive control. This motivates learning‑based robot intelligence and, in particular, Foundation Models (FMs) that can transfer knowledge across tasks, a promise attractive for high‑mix, low‑volume production. Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) are defined as models that generate low‑level actions for direct actuation, linking them tightly to industrial constraints such as latency, safety gating, and hardware‑specific action spaces.

A hierarchical control taxonomy is presented (Figure 1): (1) predefined/rule‑based, (2) reactive/parametrised, (3) specialised/narrow, (4) foundational (broadly pretrained, fine‑tunable), and (5) generalist (zero‑/few‑shot, online adaptation). The progression illustrates decreasing manual engineering and increasing flexibility, culminating in generalist systems capable of instruction‑following and safe online adaptation—capabilities still lacking for industry‑grade autonomy.

Publication trends (Figure 2) show a sharp rise in RFMs, especially in 2025, risking fragmentation and inflated claims without systematic industrial evaluation. Existing surveys address architecture but not deployment readiness. Consequently, the paper structures a review that (i) defines RFMs and situates them in the control hierarchy (Section 2), (ii) details literature acquisition and corpus composition (Section 3), (iii) surveys related work (Section 4), (iv) discusses cobot adoption and hardware constraints (Sections 5‑6), and (v) derives eleven industrial implication viewpoints and a 149‑item criteria catalogue (Section 7). Applying this framework to manipulation‑capable RFMs (Sections 8‑9) reveals that, despite benchmark progress, current models cover only a few deployment‑critical dimensions and lack integrated industrial maturity. The authors aim to shift focus from isolated benchmark successes to a traceable, implication‑grounded assessment of what constitutes a credible, industry‑ready RFM.

The authors extended their literature review beyond the two primary corpora by conducting automated and manual searches across industrial robots, cobots, compute hardware, sensors, manipulators, efficiency considerations, related fields, and relevant norms/standards. This effort yielded 113 auxiliary publications, all of which were incorporated into the study’s development and writing.

The authors built a dedicated RFM‑related literature base to cover all major research directions on robotic foundation models (RFMs) and adjacent topics such as training protocols, extensions, applications, safety and robustness. Using a standardized Python pipeline they ran two large‑scale searches (July 4 2025 and Oct 30 2025) across arXiv, Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scopus and SemanticScholar, each with eleven broad queries and a 400‑article per‑query cap, yielding up to 22 k raw hits. Search 1 returned 10 728 entries (5 035 unique); Search 2 returned 12 027 entries (4 999 unique). After merging and a conservative duplicate‑removal step the base set comprised 6 497 unique papers.

A two‑stage LLM‑driven filter first removed non‑robotics works (retaining 4 834), then filtered for RFM relevance (leaving 1 408). Manual sampling found no false negatives. Subsequent manual review, enrichment and resolution of identifier inconsistencies produced a final, highly relevant corpus of 1 025 articles, broken down as follows: 341 control or integrated RFMs (324 manipulation‑focused, 17 other domains), 321 related works (training, extensions), 231 high‑level LLM‑based or narrowly scoped models, 77 data/benchmark contributions, and 55 surveys (24 general embodied AI, 31 including RFMs, only 2 industrially focused). This curated set underpins all later analyses in the survey.

The authors built an industrial‑implication corpus using the modular pipeline of §3.1. Seven broad ASQS queries (Table B3) searched arXiv, Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scopus and Semantic Scholar for 2015‑July 2025, retrieving up to 1 750 papers. After deduplication (892 unique) a coarse LLM relevance filter left 296 relevant items; the 125 highest‑scored (≥0.9) were manually reviewed. These core articles were synthesized into industrial implications for robotics, detailed in §7.

The authors surveyed 55 recent review articles on embodied AI, classifying them by inclusion of robotic foundation models (RFMs), general‑embodied AI (GEA) and industrial focus (IND). Only 11 papers (20 % of the corpus) target RFMs, and all of these concentrate on vision‑language agents (VLAs), a single RFM sub‑category; none explicitly address industrial applications. Two surveys (3.6 % of the set) have an industrial orientation, but they limit themselves to vision‑language models for human‑robot collaboration or to broad embodied‑intelligence assessments, without discussing RFMs or their control‑oriented variants. Table 1 lists the RFM‑focused reviews, noting their scopes (architectures, challenges, datasets, tokenisation, dual‑system designs, post‑training strategies, etc.), model families (VLM, VLA, LLM, VFM) and coverage periods (typically 2014‑2025). Table 2 shows the industrial‑focused reviews, which similarly omit RFMs. The authors therefore identify a clear gap: no existing survey examines how industrial use cases shape RFMs, nor how broader RFM sub‑categories such as Vision‑Action or integrated control models should be designed and evaluated. Their contribution aims to fill this gap by providing a taxonomy, an extensive overview of the RFM landscape, and a detailed analysis of industrial requirements and maturity criteria absent from prior literature.

source_label: Section: 5 Rise of Cobots in Industry
response: The section notes that recent robot‑fabrication‑machine (RFM) advances are largely shown together with cobots, but most demonstrations remain confined to laboratory, tabletop or kitchen environments. It argues that assessing the industrial impact requires tracing the evolution from traditional industrial robots to increasingly collaborative systems, highlighting a shift toward broader, real‑world deployment.

The section notes that cobots excel at routine, ergonomic tasks but still lack autonomous handling of complex, cognitive, or dexterous work, with gaps in real‑time hazard detection, safe operation, and trustworthy HRI/HRC. It argues that foundation models (RFMs) could supply intuitive instruction, autonomous decision‑making, and adaptive reasoning via language and multisensor fusion, yet they must be proven robust beyond controlled labs in safety‑critical, variable industrial settings. The transition to collaborative robots thus both creates demand for RFMs and reveals their current limitations.

source_label: Section: 5.1 Landscape of Industrial Robotics: Tradition & Transformation
response: Industrial robots are defined as reprogrammable, multi‑axis manipulators that rely on an incomplete‑machine architecture and external tooling (e.g., grippers, welders) to perform tasks. Their complex kinematic chains give high speed, large payloads and accuracy, so they are deployed in isolated, safety‑restricted spaces for heavy, repetitive or hazardous work. Six configuration families—Delta, Cartesian, Cylindrical, SCARA, Spherical and Articulated—vary in joint types and workspace shapes, with increasing similarity to collaborative robots (cobots). Traditional robots lack the flexibility, safe direct human‑robot collaboration (HRC) and intuitive programming demanded by modern, especially SME, manufacturing. Cobots originated as passive, guided devices and have evolved into articulated robots with lower payloads, reduced speeds, rounded geometry and sensor suites for real‑time human detection. Their design emphasizes safe HRC, rapid reconfiguration, low‑cost integration and support for variable, small‑batch production, contrasting with conventional robots that aim to replace humans in isolated, high‑speed automation.

source_label: Section: 5.3 Drivers of the Industrial Shift Toward Cobots
response: The section explains a shift from manual labour and traditional industrial robots toward collaborative robots (cobots) driven by technological, organisational and economic factors. Traditional robots excel in high‑volume, repetitive tasks but are costly, complex and hard to reconfigure, limiting suitability for SMEs that need low‑volume, high‑mix production. Cobots address these gaps with flexible design, compact size, easy programming and user‑friendly interfaces, reducing specialist expertise and integration time. They aim to assist humans on repetitive, hazardous work, improve safety, and enable direct human‑robot collaboration through sensors, force/torque monitoring and adaptive behaviour, lowering the need for safety cages. Research and market data show rapid growth: cobot‑focused publications rose over five‑fold in a decade, annual installations grew from 11 000 in 2017 to 55 000 in 2022, and their share of global robot deployments is increasing. Advances in computer vision and adaptive control further extend cobot capabilities, aligning with Industry 4.0 goals of flexible, connected, and data‑driven manufacturing.

Cobots, thanks to greater flexibility and safety than traditional robots, have moved from labs into diverse real‑world sectors. In manufacturing they handle precision‑critical, adaptable tasks such as assembly, pick‑and‑place, machine tending, inspection, palletising, packaging, welding and gluing; examples include UR10e units at PSA and Fiat Chrysler for door, hood and soft‑top assembly and rivetting. Quality control leverages vision sensors for real‑time dimension, integrity and defect checks, e.g., UR3 inspection of automotive touchscreen panels. Integrated with AMRs, cobots form mobile manipulators for intra‑factory logistics, exemplified by MiR200 moving components in appliance production. In healthcare they aid patient handling, rehabilitation, medication dispensing and surgical assistance. Agriculture uses them for precise planting, harvesting and sorting, reducing seasonal labour. Retail and service employ cobots for shelf stocking, object retrieval and customer interaction. Military, security and inspection applications include luggage scanning, hazardous substance detection, bomb disposal, facility inspection, cleaning and spacecraft surface maintenance, with documented use on the Space Rider orbiter and border inspections.

The section outlines hardware prerequisites for deploying RFMs with cobots, noting that current cobots lack autonomous handling of complex tasks. It surveys cobot reach, payload, accuracy, power use, and perception/manipulation hardware (6.1), then reviews industrial edge computing platforms for real‑time inference (6.3), and details required sensors and manipulators (6.2). This frames the technical baseline for integrating RFMs in industry.

Sensors are the primary means for cobot perception and self‑monitoring, covering visual (RGB, depth, CCD, 2D/3D), range (LiDAR, RADAR, sonar, ultrasonic, TOF/PMD, laser), dynamics (IMU, gyroscope, accelerometer, force/torque, tactile, pressure), position/identification (encoders, RFID, infrared, GPS, odometry, magnetic) and specialised (acoustic, thermal) modalities. Advanced RFMs exploit sensor fusion—e.g., vision with proximity, inertial or force/torque—to boost robustness, safety and compliance, often using redundant or complementary setups such as visual‑tactile feedback for precise handling. End‑effectors (grippers, suction cups, dual‑stage tools, custom drills/polishers) frequently embed sensors (force feedback, vision) and are modular for rapid task reconfiguration, though this assumes equally flexible control‑action spaces. The breadth of sensing and manipulation hardware expands observation‑action permutations, underscoring the need for multimodal, output‑flexible control algorithms central to RFMs.

The section outlines how industrial deployment adds heterogeneous hardware, safety, compliance, reliability and continuous operation constraints that differ from labs. It extracts eleven domain‑agnostic industrial implications from the implication corpus, maps them to detailed attributes for RFM ecosystems, and assembles a criteria catalogue to evaluate industrial maturity of current and future RFMs.

The section quantifies contemporary articulated anthropomorphic cobots using data from Taesi et al. [50]. Across 180 models, the mean degree‑of‑freedom count is 6.09, confirming six‑axis designs dominate collaborative use. Payloads average 8.56 kg (median 5.5 kg), with extreme outliers up to 170 kg; typical reach is about 910 mm (mean 970 mm) and positioning accuracy centers on 0.05 mm (mean 0.09 mm). For the 63 models rated 0.5–20 kg, peak TCP speed spans 0.2–6 m s⁻¹ (median 1.1 m s⁻¹, mean 1.68 m s⁻¹) and power draw ranges 0.06–0.9 kW (median 0.25 kW, mean 0.31 kW). Compared with conventional industrial robots (≈3 kW average, peaks ≥12 kW), cobots consume markedly less energy, supporting lower‑cost operation, deployment in limited‑power settings, and mobile or battery‑powered platforms. Consequently, real‑time RFM deployment must prioritize models that fit these constrained energy budgets and maintain low‑latency inference.

The authors translate eleven industry‑level implications for robot foundation models (RFMs) into a structured set of deployment‑relevant attributes. After reviewing the qualitative observations of Section 7.1, they define 47 attributes spanning hardware, sensing, actions, safety, security, adaptability, compliance, real‑time performance, governance and related concerns (Table 7). An iterative mapping pairs each implication with every attribute, yielding 517 implication‑attribute cells that capture specific industrial constraints and failure modes. This matrix highlights the interdependence of requirements—e.g., safety links to perception, real‑time feasibility to interaction, and robustness to fault handling. The resulting attribute catalogue serves as an intermediate, traceable representation for the criteria catalogue in Section 7.3 and underpins the forthcoming assessment framework for industrial‑readiness of RFMs. The full matrix is omitted for brevity, and Table 7’s reconstruction is noted as unreliable.

Industrial cobot control demands ultra‑low latency, so AI‑enabled perception and control are typically placed on edge PCs that sit as close as possible to the robot’s sensors and controller.  Edge devices process data locally, avoiding the network‑induced delays of fog or cloud architectures, which, while scalable, require additional infrastructure and incur higher latency, lower throughput, and greater risk of service interruption.  Recent industrial trends favour moving computation to the edge because compute costs are falling and networking expenses are reduced.

The section surveys currently available edge hardware, focusing on NVIDIA Jetson devices because their performance, pricing and specifications are publicly documented across the whole product line.  Table 6 lists Jetson models from the low‑cost Nano series up to the high‑end Thor series, together with a desktop‑class RTX 5090 used as a performance reference.  Prices reflect single‑unit purchases from an NVIDIA‑specified retailer; power draws are measured at typical operating points; operational cost assumes 24 h/day use at 0.25 $/kWh.

Key quantitative findings: the Orin Nano devices deliver the highest TOPS‑per‑dollar (≈148 TOPS $/) and low power (≈25 W), making them attractive for large‑scale, cost‑sensitive deployments.  The entry‑level Xavier NX, despite a higher price, provides the lowest absolute AI compute (≈21 TOPS) but also the lowest maximum power (≈15 W), suiting energy‑constrained applications.  Mid‑tier Orin AGX 32 GB balances capability (200 TOPS) with moderate power (≈40 W) and achieves the best compute‑per‑operational‑cost ratio (≈200 $/year).  High‑end Thor devices and the RTX 5090 reach >500 TOPS but consume >120 W and incur annual energy costs > $300, limiting their suitability for mobile or battery‑powered cobots.

Industrial‑class (IND) variants add ECC memory for reliability, which raises both purchase price and operational cost while sometimes reducing raw compute compared with research‑grade equivalents.  Overall, the analysis underscores a trade‑off: larger, more capable robotic foundation models must be matched to edge hardware that satisfies both compute throughput and energy‑efficiency constraints to be viable in real‑world industrial settings.

The section surveys 324 manipulation‑capable RFMs, rating each against 149 implication‑grounded criteria (48,276 decisions) to produce overall maturity scores and implication‑wise profiles. It details the scalable evaluation method (8.1) and validates it with 28 expert judgments on a ground‑truth subset. Results highlight top‑performing models (8.2) and assess industrial applicability for the full set and a Top‑50 subset (8.3), forming the basis for the maturity characterization and outlook.

source_label: Section: 7.3 Evaluating Industrial Maturity: A Criteria Catalogue
response:
The section translates the eleven industrial implications for robotic foundation models (RFMs) into a concrete assessment tool. Building on 517 implication‑attribute pairs, the authors distilled 149 questions into a “criteria catalogue” (Table C4) that spans model capabilities, ecosystem requirements, and joint model‑ecosystem functions. Criteria address adaptive behavior under distribution shifts, failure detection and handling, human‑input interpretation, and audit‑ready artefacts. Although most items target the RFM itself, many require supporting software stacks, safety infrastructure, logging, and documentation; the catalogue therefore classifies criteria as model‑centric, ecosystem‑centric, or hybrid.

Redundancy is intentional: the same functional requirement (e.g., hot‑swapping) appears under multiple implications with distinct industrial emphases, preserving diagnostic granularity. The catalogue is organized around several research paradigms that already have emerging literature but are not yet combined in practice. These include: (1) multi‑hardware support and runtime adaptation to changing observation/action spaces, with recent work on unified action representations and variable‑size interfaces; (2) robustness to out‑of‑distribution and adversarial scenarios, citing evidence of textual and visual attacks that can compromise VLAs and the need for online detection, confidence signaling, and fallback policies; (3) calibrated uncertainty and confidence measures to trigger help‑seeking, halting, or escalation, supported by confidence‑calibration studies for VLAs and LLM‑based planners; (4) interactive clarification and human‑in‑the‑loop correction, where recent methods generate follow‑up questions or allow trajectory adjustments via natural language; (5) decoupled supervisory layers for safety gating and failure detection across tasks, with VLM‑based reactive monitoring and task‑agnostic detectors; and (6) memory, data governance, and documentation, where lightweight memory modules improve long‑horizon performance and privacy‑preserving training addresses regulatory constraints.

The authors argue that most catalogue items correspond to active research threads; the gap to industrial maturity lies in integrating these pieces into a systematic, auditable, safety‑governed RFM ecosystem. The catalogue thus serves as a living framework to evaluate current RFMs, pinpoint immaturity dimensions, and guide future work toward credible industrial deployment.

The authors performed an iterative qualitative synthesis of 125 manually reviewed industrial works to extract recurring requirements for robotic systems. By extracting statements about industrial needs, clustering them thematically, and refining the clusters, they derived eleven inter‑dependent implications that capture dominant industrial viewpoints while remaining actionable for assessing robot foundation models (RFMs).

1. **Adaptability & Flexibility** – Across domains, real deployments are characterized by frequent process changes, product variants, and dynamic, partially known environments. Traditional automation is brittle under such variation, so robots must adjust behavior online, be reconfigurable across tasks and embodiments, and reduce costly re‑programming, especially when humans share the workspace or conditions such as lighting and weather vary.

2. **Safety & Compliance** – Safety is a gating factor, particularly for collaborative robots (cobots) in shared spaces. Industrial deployment must satisfy standards (e.g., ISO‑10218, ISO/TS‑15066) and maintain safety under dynamic, uncertain conditions, without overly conservative stops that hurt productivity. Certification and robust safety‑aware reasoning are required.

3. **Human‑Robot Interaction & Collaboration (HRI/HRC)** – Future industrial robotics is envisioned as human‑centric, demanding diverse interaction regimes (coexistence, cooperation, collaboration) and natural, intuitive interfaces (speech, multimodal cues). Systems must enable operators to instruct, supervise, and correct robots directly, handling uncertainty to keep workflows fluid.

4. **Robustness & Reliability** – Environments are noisy, uncertain, and prone to sensor faults, adversarial attacks, and out‑of‑distribution inputs. Robust methods must integrate perception, planning, and control under these disturbances, provide fault awareness, and support reactive planning.

5. **Precision & Accuracy** – High precision, repeatability, and accurate perception are essential for quality‑critical tasks and competitive throughput. Gaps between household‑style demonstrations and industrial needs highlight the need for improved motion planning and sensing accuracy.

6. **Real‑Time Performance** – Tight latency bounds are required for sensing, decision‑making, and control, even on edge devices with limited compute and energy budgets. Real‑time perception and planning remain challenging, especially for vision‑language‑action pipelines.

7. **Cost‑Effectiveness & Integration** – Automation must be economically justified, especially for low‑volume production and SMEs. Solutions should lower commissioning effort, integrate smoothly into existing factory architectures, and run on cost‑sensitive hardware.

8. **Explainability & Trust** – Transparency and interpretable outputs are crucial for operator acceptance, safety‑critical contexts, and collaborative work. Explainable AI and user‑friendly interfaces help build trust and mitigate fear of failure.

9. **Sensor Fusion & Perception** – Single modalities are insufficient; multi‑modal sensing and fusion are needed to handle occlusions, lighting changes, and sensor degradation, supporting robust perception for safe HRC and dynamic environments.

10. **Standardised Benchmarking & Evaluation** – Reproducible, task‑relevant benchmarks and metrics are required to compare systems, validate performance, and enable digital‑twin testing, addressing the current lack of unified standards.

11. **Data Requirements & Usage** – Industrial settings face data scarcity, costly collection, and simulation‑to‑real gaps. Methods must be data‑efficient (few‑shot, continual learning) and support large‑scale multimodal datasets while reducing compute demands.

These implications are presented not merely as desirable traits but as bottlenecks that explain why many laboratory‑grade learning approaches fail to translate to production. They form the basis for the subsequent analysis of which RFM attributes satisfy industrial readiness and for the development of an assessment framework.

The authors evaluated industrial readiness for every manipulation‑capable robot‑foundation model (RFM) in their corpus—324 papers out of 341 total—against a catalogue of 149 implication‑grounded criteria, producing 48 276 criterion‑paper decisions. Because manual annotation at this scale was infeasible, they built an automated pipeline that queries a large language model (GPT‑5.1) for each single criterion‑paper pair in strict isolation: the LLM receives only that criterion and a vector‑store containing the full text of the target paper, then outputs a binary fulfilment judgment, a direct‑statement flag, a confidence score, an evidence‑availability flag, extracted quotes, and a brief rationale. The pipeline enforces independence by deleting the vector store and closing the session after each query, preventing cross‑paper or cross‑criterion leakage. All processing occurred on private Siemens infrastructure, avoiding public upload or training use.

To gauge reliability, the authors compared LLM outputs to expert annotations on three representative papers (two pre‑run, one post‑run). At the criterion level (N = 447), the LLM achieved 96.6 % accuracy, F1 = 0.762 for the positive class, Cohen’s κ = 0.744, a low false‑positive rate (1.9 %) and a higher false‑negative rate (22.6 %) reflecting its conservative policy. Per‑paper agreement was strong for Gemini Robotics 1.5 and OpenVLA, but lower for π0 due to the rarity of positive labels (expert positive rate = 2.7 %). Disagreements often stemmed from interpretive ambiguity in criteria (e.g., “low‑data adaptation” thresholds or “always” guarantees) rather than outright errors.

Overall, the authors conclude the pipeline yields reliable, lower‑bound maturity estimates suitable for corpus‑scale comparison and implication‑level analysis, while advising caution for fine‑grained, criterion‑level interpretations because of the higher miss rate and criterion ambiguity.

The authors iteratively synthesized 125 industrial case studies into eleven inter‑dependent implications that define the dominant requirements for deploying learning‑based robot control and foundation‑model approaches: (1) systems must be adaptable, flexible, safe, and compliant, supporting human‑centric interaction, high precision, real‑time operation, cost‑effective integration, explainable behavior, robust multi‑modal perception, standardized benchmarking, and data‑efficient learning despite limited, noisy, and heterogeneous data; (2) these themes are repeatedly cited as bottlenecks that cause laboratory‑grade methods to fail in production, linking each requirement to specific industrial constraints such as dynamic environments, safety standards, computational budgets, and integration obstacles; (3) the eleven implications form the basis for assessing robotic foundation models’ industrial readiness in the subsequent sections.

The authors evaluated 324 robot‑functioning models (RFMs) against an implication‑grounded industrial maturity framework.  The five top‑scoring models (Table 11) achieved total proportional applicability scores of only 0.11–0.12, meaning they satisfy roughly one‑tenth of the catalogue criteria on average.  The ceiling effect is pronounced: even the strongest model, Gemini Robotics 1.5 [157], reaches a total score of 0.12 and the highest single‑implication value of 0.44 for adaptability/flexibility (I1).  No model exceeds 0.44 on any implication, and most scores are clustered near zero, indicating that current RFMs address only narrow subsets of industrial requirements.

A common pattern among the best models is the use of multi‑component architectures that isolate high‑level reasoning, human‑in‑the‑loop guidance, self‑correction, or enhanced perception from low‑level action generation.  For example, Gemini Robotics 1.5 combines a visual‑language agent (VLA) with a visual‑language model (VLM) to form a hybrid framework, while OneTwo VLA [6] alternates between a fast “System One” and a slower “System Two” reasoning mode.  SC‑VLA [160] integrates fast action prediction with a reflective correction mechanism, yielding the highest scores for robustness (I4 = 0.21) and precision (I5 = 0.23).  Collab‑VLA [158] and GF‑VLA [159] score highest on human‑robot interaction (I1 = 0.28) and data‑usage (I11 = 0.27) respectively, reflecting their explicit focus on collaborative agents and demonstration learning.

Agreement between expert and LLM‑based evaluations was strong: across 447 implication assessments the overall accuracy was 96.6 % (F1 = 0.762, κ = 0.744), with a false‑positive rate of 1.9 % but a higher false‑negative rate of 22.6 %.  Per‑paper agreement mirrored this pattern, with Gemini 1.5 showing the highest positive‑class Jaccard (0.714) despite a low positive rate (12 %).  Tables 8–10 could not be reliably reconstructed, so numeric details from those tables are omitted.

The per‑implication maxima (Table 12) show that many different works share the highest score of 0.11 for I6 (data efficiency), while other implications are dominated by single models (e.g., I1 = 0.44 for Gemini 1.5, I2 = 0.39 for Sirius‑Fleet Smol).  Overall, the landscape reveals a trend toward optimizing one or two bottlenecks rather than delivering integrated, industry‑grade solutions.  The authors conclude that, although recent RFMs begin to address specific industrial concerns, none yet achieve comprehensive coverage of the full implication set, and further research is needed to build layered systems that combine high‑level reasoning, verification, and interaction with robust low‑level control.

The section evaluates how well recent robot‑foundation‑model (RFM) papers address industrial‑relevant implications. Using all 324 evaluated works and a high‑performing Top‑50 subset, the authors examine temporal stability, breadth versus depth of coverage, the most frequently fulfilled criteria, and the gap between discussion and actual fulfilment.

**Temporal stability** (Fig. 11) shows a consistent pattern across 2020‑2025: a small set of implications dominates the literature while others stay low. The most addressed are adaptability/flexibility (I1), benchmarking/evaluation (I10) and data requirements/usage (I11). Safety/compliance (I2), human‑robot interaction (I3), real‑time performance (I6) and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7) remain under‑represented. No implication shows a monotonic increase, indicating the field is not moving toward broader industrial coverage but rather deepening a stable set of emphases.

**Breadth vs. depth** (Fig. 12, Table 13) contrasts two metrics per implication: 1⁺‑Coverage (share of papers meeting at least one criterion) and Average Criteria Coverage (ACC, average fraction of criteria met). Across the full corpus, only I1 (0.756), I10 (0.753) and I11 (0.707) achieve high breadth; their ACC values stay below 0.10 (I10 0.099, I11 0.097, I1 0.089). Safety/compliance (I2 0.034), HRI/HRC (I3 0.052), real‑time performance (I6 0.049) and cost‑effectiveness (I7 0.071) have very low breadth. The Top‑50 subset raises breadth to near‑universal for several implications (e.g., I1, I4‑I5, I8‑I11 at 1.0) and improves depth (ACC up to 0.238 for I1, 0.232 for I10, 0.227 for I11), yet safety (I2 0.019) and real‑time (I6 0.036) remain low.

**Most frequently fulfilled criteria** (Table 14) cluster in the three well‑covered implications. The top ten include Multi‑Task Generalisation (I1, 49 % fulfilment), Flexible Data Type Acceptance (I11, 48 %), Repeatability & Reproducibility (I10, 45 %), and Low‑Data Adaptation & Few‑Shot Requirements (I11, 42 %). Explicitness of fulfilment is modest for some (e.g., Multi‑Task Generalisation 0.28), higher for others (Low‑Data Adaptation 0.81), suggesting many claims are inferred rather than directly stated.

**Evidence‑fulfilled gap** (Table 15) computes a gap score gc = EvidRate − FulfillRate for the highest‑evidence criterion per implication. Gaps are large (often > 0.8), meaning criteria are frequently discussed or documented but rarely satisfied under the binary fulfilment policy. Notably, safety/compliance (I2) and real‑time performance (I6) have very low fulfilment despite high evidence rates.

Overall, the analysis indicates that RFM research increasingly acknowledges industrial constraints but still delivers limited, criterion‑incomplete solutions. Breadth is modest and depth remains shallow, especially for implications critical to deployment (safety, real‑time operation, cost‑effectiveness, HRI/HRC). Even the strongest papers (Top‑50) improve coverage but do not achieve comprehensive industrial maturity.

Industrial robotics is shifting from isolated, highly tuned automation to flexible, collaborative cobot deployments where humans share workspaces. This transition is driven by cobots’ safe design, suitable payloads, and low power, yet the core bottleneck remains robust, deployment‑ready intelligence that can adapt to changing tasks, environments, and multimodal inputs without heavy engineering effort. The authors argue that robot foundation models (RFMs) uniquely address this need by targeting multi‑task competence, cross‑domain generalisation, and low‑effort reconfiguration, areas where classical control and specialised learning fall short.

Across the corpus, research consistently focuses on adaptability, benchmarking, and data usage, while safety/compliance, HRI/HRC, real‑time performance, and cost‑effectiveness remain under‑represented. The authors conclude that progress is driven by isolated bottleneck solutions rather than holistic, industry‑grade integration. They recommend moving toward layered architectures with testable planning, verification, and safety components; developing evaluation protocols that reflect edge latency, logging, and changing sensor/tooling; and leveraging benchmarking to assess distribution shifts, failure recovery, and long‑horizon operation. Closing gaps in safety, HRI/HRC, real‑time capability, and integration is essential for RFMs to become reliable, auditable, and deployable in cobot‑centred automation.

Across 324 evaluated robotic foundation models, the five highest‑rated systems achieve total maturity scores of only 0.11–0.12, meaning they satisfy roughly one‑tenth of the catalogue’s industrial implications; the strongest single implication score is 0.44 for adaptability/flexibility (I1) by Gemini Robotics 1.5, while all other implications remain below 0.33 and many are near zero, indicating that current RFMs address only narrow, often single‑dimension bottlenecks such as structured reasoning, human‑in‑the‑loop guidance, self‑correction, or perception/data use rather than providing integrated, industry‑grade coverage. The paper opens by positioning industrial robotics at a crossroads: traditional, high‑speed, fixed‑automation systems are giving way to collaborative robots (cobots) that must be commissioned quickly, redeployed across changing processes, and operate safely alongside humans. Mechanical performance is no longer the bottleneck; instead, robust, adaptive, and intuitive control is. This motivates the emergence of learning‑based robot intelligence, specifically Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs), which are defined as models that generate low‑level actions for direct actuation while respecting industrial constraints such as latency, safety gating, and hardware‑specific action spaces.

A hierarchical taxonomy of robot control is introduced, ranging from predefined rule‑based systems to reactive parametrised controllers, specialised narrow models, foundational pretrained‑and‑fine‑tunable models, and finally generalist systems capable of zero‑ or few‑shot online adaptation. The authors argue that only the generalist tier currently lacks the safety‑critical, online‑adaptation capabilities required for industry‑grade autonomy. Publication trends show a rapid rise in RFMs, especially in 2025, raising concerns about fragmented claims and a lack of systematic industrial evaluation. Existing surveys focus on architecture but not on deployment readiness, prompting the authors to structure their review around five goals: defining RFMs within the control hierarchy, detailing literature acquisition, surveying related work, discussing cobot adoption and hardware constraints, and deriving industrial implication viewpoints and a 149‑item criteria catalogue for assessing industrial maturity.

RFMs are presented as the robotic counterpart of large‑scale foundation models in language and vision. A true RFM must combine (1) multi‑modality (proprioception, images, natural‑language instructions), (2) output flexibility (actions, plans, trajectories for diverse robots), and (3) adaptability (cross‑task, cross‑embodiment generalisation via prompts, goal images, demonstrations, or lightweight fine‑tuning). The authors distinguish single‑purpose RFMs (focused on perception, planning, or control) from general‑purpose RFMs that integrate perception with actionable outputs, and treat Vision‑Language‑Action (VLA) models as a sub‑category that aligns vision, language, and action into a common token format for end‑to‑end training. Taxonomically, RFMs are grouped into control‑oriented models (low‑level motor commands), planning‑oriented models (high‑level task decompositions), and integrated models that jointly plan and control, representing the most ambitious step toward general robotic intelligence. Models qualify as RFMs when they demonstrably transcend narrow, hardware‑specific solutions, offering cross‑task, cross‑embodiment flexibility while handling heterogeneous sensory inputs and producing versatile outputs.

The review methodology is fully reproducible. An automated Python pipeline retrieves articles from arXiv, Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scopus, and Semantic Scholar using structured Academic Search Query Syntax (ASQS) queries, applies duplicate removal, fills missing metadata via auxiliary APIs, and validates title‑abstract consistency. A GPT‑4o filter scores semantic relevance, providing binary labels, a 0‑1 relevance score, and rationales; filters can be chained for stricter selection. After automated steps, two manual refinement stages ensure completeness and relevance. This workflow yields three corpora: a main RFM‑related set (81.2 % of total), an industrial‑implication set (9.9 %), and a further auxiliary set (8.9 %), together comprising 1,263 publications.

The RFM‑related corpus was built from two large‑scale searches (July 4 2025 and Oct 30 2025) with eleven broad queries each, capped at 400 results per query, producing up to 22 k raw hits. After merging, duplicate removal, and a two‑stage LLM‑driven filter (first removing non‑robotics works, then selecting RFM relevance), the final curated set contains 1,025 highly relevant papers. These break down into 341 control or integrated RFMs (324 manipulation‑focused), 321 works on training and extensions, 231 high‑level LLM‑based or narrowly scoped models, 77 data/benchmark contributions, and 55 surveys (only two with an industrial focus). The industrial‑implication corpus was assembled from seven broad queries covering 2015‑July 2025, yielding 892 unique papers; after a coarse LLM relevance filter, 125 high‑scoring items were manually reviewed and synthesized into eleven domain‑agnostic industrial implications (Section 7). An additional 113 auxiliary publications on cobots, compute hardware, sensors, manipulators, efficiency, standards, and related fields were incorporated to enrich the analysis.

Related‑work analysis reveals a clear gap: among 55 recent embodied‑AI surveys, only 11 (20 %) address RFMs, all focusing exclusively on VLAs, and none discuss industrial applications. Only two surveys have an industrial orientation, but they also omit RFMs. Consequently, no existing review examines how industrial use cases shape RFMs or how broader sub‑categories such as Vision‑Action or integrated control models should be designed and evaluated. The authors aim to fill this gap with a taxonomy, a comprehensive overview of the RFM landscape, and a detailed industrial‑requirements analysis.

The cobot landscape is described in detail. Traditional industrial robots are high‑speed, high‑payload, multi‑axis manipulators deployed in isolated, safety‑restricted spaces for repetitive, hazardous work. Cobots have evolved from passive guided devices to articulated robots with lower payloads, reduced speeds, rounded geometry, and sensor suites for real‑time human detection. Their design emphasizes safe human‑robot collaboration (HRC), rapid reconfiguration, low‑cost integration, and support for variable, small‑batch production, making them attractive to SMEs. Real‑world deployments span manufacturing (assembly, pick‑and‑place, machine tending, inspection, packaging, welding, gluing), logistics (mobile manipulators with AMRs), healthcare (patient handling, rehabilitation, medication dispensing, surgical assistance), agriculture (planting, harvesting, sorting), retail and service (shelf stocking, object retrieval), and security/military (hazard detection, bomb disposal, spacecraft maintenance). Drivers of this shift include the high cost and inflexibility of traditional robots, the need for flexible, user‑friendly programming, and the desire for direct HRC to improve safety and ergonomics. Publication and installation data show a five‑fold increase in cobot‑focused papers over a decade and a rise from 11 000 installations in 2017 to 55 000 in 2022, aligning with Industry 4.0 goals of flexible, connected, data‑driven manufacturing.

Despite these advances, cobots still lack autonomous handling of complex, cognitive, or dexterous tasks. The authors argue that RFMs could provide intuitive instruction, autonomous decision‑making, and adaptive reasoning via language and multisensor fusion, but they must be proven robust beyond controlled labs in safety‑critical, variable industrial settings.

Hardware prerequisites for deploying RFMs with cobots are surveyed. Across 180 articulated cobot models, the mean degree‑of‑freedom count is 6.09, average payload 8.56 kg (median 5.5 kg), typical reach ≈910 mm, and positioning accuracy ≈0.05 mm. For the 63 models rated 0.5–20 kg, peak TCP speed ranges 0.2–6 m s⁻¹ (median 1.1 m s⁻¹) and power draw 0.06–0.9 kW (median 0.25 kW), markedly lower than conventional industrial robots (≈3 kW average, peaks ≥12 kW). Consequently, RFM deployment must respect constrained energy budgets and low‑latency inference requirements.

A broad sensor suite underpins cobot perception: visual (RGB, depth), range (LiDAR, radar, sonar), dynamics (IMU, force/torque, tactile), position/identification (encoders, RFID, GPS), and specialised modalities (acoustic, thermal). Advanced RFMs exploit sensor fusion (e.g., vision‑tactile feedback) to improve robustness, safety, and compliance, often using modular end‑effectors that embed force or vision sensors, thereby expanding observation‑action permutations and reinforcing the need for multimodal, output‑flexible control algorithms.

Real‑time inference is typically placed on industrial edge PCs to avoid network latency. The survey focuses on NVIDIA Jetson devices, presenting a cost‑performance analysis across Nano, Xavier, Orin, and Thor series, with a desktop‑class RTX 5090 as reference. Orin Nano offers the highest TOPS‑per‑dollar (≈148 TOPS $/) at ≈25 W, suitable for large‑scale, cost‑sensitive deployments. Xavier NX provides the lowest absolute AI compute (≈21 TOPS) and power (≈15 W), fitting energy‑constrained scenarios. Mid‑tier Orin AGX 32 GB balances capability (200 TOPS) with moderate power (≈40 W) and achieves the best compute‑per‑operational‑cost ratio (≈200 $/year). High‑end Thor devices and RTX 5090 exceed 500 TOPS but consume >120 W and incur > $300 annual energy cost, limiting suitability for mobile or battery‑powered cobots. Industrial‑class variants add ECC memory for reliability, raising price and operational cost while sometimes reducing raw compute. The analysis underscores a trade‑off: larger, more capable RFMs must be matched to edge hardware that satisfies both throughput and energy‑efficiency constraints.

From the industrial‑implication corpus, eleven inter‑dependent implications are synthesized, covering adaptability, flexibility, safety, compliance, human‑centric interaction, high precision, real‑time operation, cost‑effective integration, explainability, robust multimodal perception, standardized benchmarking, and data‑efficient learning under limited, noisy, heterogeneous data. These themes are repeatedly cited as bottlenecks that cause laboratory‑grade methods to fail in production, linking each requirement to specific industrial constraints such as dynamic environments, safety standards, computational budgets, and integration obstacles.

These eleven implications are mapped to 47 deployment‑relevant attributes (hardware, sensing, actions, safety, security, adaptability, compliance, real‑time performance, governance, etc.), yielding a matrix of 517 implication‑attribute cells that capture specific industrial constraints and failure modes. Although the full matrix is omitted and noted as unreliably reconstructed, it serves as the basis for a 149‑item criteria catalogue. The catalogue classifies items as model‑centric, ecosystem‑centric, or hybrid, and addresses adaptive behavior under distribution shifts, failure detection, human‑input interpretation, audit‑ready artefacts, multi‑hardware support, robustness to out‑of‑distribution and adversarial attacks, calibrated uncertainty for safe escalation, interactive clarification, decoupled supervisory safety layers, and memory/data governance. Redundancy is intentional to preserve diagnostic granularity across multiple implications.

To evaluate current RFMs, the authors surveyed 324 manipulation‑capable models (out of 341 control/integrated RFMs) against the 149‑item catalogue, generating 48 276 binary decisions. Manual annotation at this scale was infeasible, so an automated pipeline queried a large language model (GPT‑5.1) for each criterion‑paper pair in isolation, providing a binary fulfilment judgment, a direct‑statement flag, confidence score, evidence‑availability flag, extracted quotes, and rationale. The authors set out to map the current state of robot‑foundation models (RFMs) against a systematic catalogue of industrial‑deployment criteria.  Their motivation is the emerging shift in manufacturing from tightly programmed, single‑task automation toward collaborative cobots that must operate safely alongside humans, adapt to changing tasks, and run on low‑power edge hardware.  To evaluate whether existing RFMs can meet these demands, the study first defined eleven inter‑dependent industrial implications (I1‑I11) and expanded them into 47 concrete deployment attributes, yielding a detailed criteria catalogue of 149 items that span model capabilities, ecosystem requirements, safety, human‑robot interaction, real‑time performance, cost‑efficiency, explainability, and data usage.  The catalogue was applied to a literature corpus of 324 papers describing manipulation‑capable RFMs, representing 48 276 individual criterion decisions.

**Scope of the literature search**  
Appendix B documents the exact Boolean search strings used to assemble two corpora: one targeting RFM‑related work (eleven “ASQS” queries) and another targeting industrial‑implication literature (seven queries).  The queries combined robot‑centric terms with “foundation model”, “large‑scale AI”, “multimodal”, “vision‑language‑action”, and, for the industrial set, descriptors such as “industrial”, “automation”, “safety”, and “regulation”.  Although the tabular layout of the queries could not be fully reconstructed, the full textual strings are provided, ensuring transparency of the retrieval process.

**Industrial‑implication framework**  
Appendix C enumerates the full set of criteria.  Adaptability (I1) requires hardware‑agnostic operation, multimodal interaction, autonomous fault handling and self‑explanation.  Verification, standards and safety (I2) demand demonstrable compliance, real‑time safety monitoring, redundant gating and transparent logging.  Human‑robot interaction (I3) calls for multimodal instruction, confidence‑driven clarification, privacy‑preserving data handling and adaptive teammate behaviour.  Robustness (I4) includes multi‑level fault detection, reproducible diagnosis, graceful degradation and continuous learning.  Precision, accuracy and repeatability (I5) expect explicit targets, confidence scoring, experience‑based improvement and verification modules.  Real‑time operation (I6) insists on deterministic timing, dynamic resource management and live metric reporting.  Cost‑efficiency (I7) emphasizes low‑cost hardware, dynamic allocation, hot‑swap detection and extensive documentation.  Explainability (I8) requires clear feasibility explanations, logging, multimodal interfaces and security‑compliant reporting.  Sensor fusion (I9) obliges real‑time multimodal integration, fault‑tolerant weighting, online perception learning and modular benchmarking.  Meta‑criteria (I10‑A to I10‑D) prescribe evaluation on diverse, standardized benchmarks covering task breadth, hardware‑aware resource use, repeatable robustness testing, multimodal command interpretation, module‑level skill assessment, safety, explainability and autonomous self‑evaluation.  Data‑efficiency criteria (I11‑A to I11‑E) demand few‑shot or zero‑shot adaptation, broad pre‑training with documented sim‑to‑real transfer, automatic data‑sufficiency feedback, privacy‑compliant usage reporting and confidence‑scored fine‑tuning.  The authors note that numeric tables for these items could not be reliably reconstructed, so quantitative comparisons are limited to the summary statistics they report.

**Quantitative assessment of RFMs**  
Using an LLM‑based pipeline (Section 8.1), each of the 324 RFMs was assigned a total industrial‑applicability proportion and eleven implication‑specific scores.  All total scores are ≤ 0.12, with the majority ≤ 0.05, indicating that, on average, a model satisfies roughly one‑tenth of the catalogue’s criteria.  The five highest‑rated systems reach total maturity scores of only 0.11–0.12; the strongest single‑implication score is 0.44 for adaptability/flexibility (I1) achieved by Gemini Robotics 1.5.  All other implication scores remain below 0.33, many approaching zero.  The top models typically excel in only two or three implications—most often adaptability (I1), robustness (I4), sensor fusion (I9) or data usage (I11)—while scoring near zero on safety/compliance (I2), human‑robot interaction (I3), real‑time performance (I6) and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7).  Expert‑LLM agreement on these assessments is high (overall accuracy 0.966, κ 0.744), but the underlying tables could not be fully reconstructed, so the reported aggregate numbers are the only reliable quantitative evidence.

**Breadth–depth analysis of the literature**  
Section 8.3 expands the picture by examining how often each industrial implication appears in the 324 papers and how deeply it is addressed.  Over the 2020‑2025 period, research consistently concentrates on three implications: adaptability/flexibility (I1), benchmarking/evaluation (I10) and data requirements/usage (I11).  Coverage metrics show that many papers mention these dominant implications (≈ 0.75 of papers for each), yet the average criteria coverage (ACC) stays below 0.10, meaning that only a small fraction of the detailed items within each implication are actually fulfilled.  Even when restricting to the top‑50 most cited papers, breadth improves to near‑universal mention of I1, I10 and I11, but depth remains modest (ACC ≈ 0.23 for those three).  Safety/compliance (I2), HRI/HRC (I3), real‑time performance (I6) and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7) are persistently under‑addressed, with ACC values below 0.05.  Gap analysis reveals a pattern: criteria are frequently discussed (high EvidRate) but rarely realized (large gap‑count, gc), especially for deployment‑critical implications.  This mismatch underscores a systemic focus on acknowledging industrial constraints without delivering concrete solutions.

**Contextual discussion and conclusions**  
The summary (Section 9) interprets these findings against the backdrop of cobot deployment requirements.  While cobots offer safe design, moderate payload (0.5‑20 kg) and low median power, they impose strict constraints on inference latency, energy consumption, and adaptability to heterogeneous sensor and actuator configurations.  The authors argue that RFMs are uniquely positioned to address the need for multi‑task competence, cross‑domain generalisation, and low‑effort reconfiguration—areas where classical control pipelines and specialised learning methods fall short.  However, the empirical evidence shows that current RFMs deliver only isolated bottleneck solutions: they may provide flexible reasoning or data‑efficient learning but lack integrated safety monitoring, real‑time deterministic execution, and cost‑effective hardware integration.  Consequently, no model yet offers a holistic, industry‑grade solution.

The authors recommend a shift toward layered architectures that separate planning, verification, and safety components, enabling testable modules that can be independently validated.  They also call for evaluation protocols that reflect edge‑latency constraints, logging requirements, and dynamic sensor/tooling changes, and for benchmarking suites that assess distribution shifts, failure recovery, and long‑horizon operation.  Closing the gaps in safety/compliance (I2), human‑robot interaction (I3), real‑time capability (I6) and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7) is identified as essential for RFMs to become reliable, auditable and deployable in cobot‑centred automation.

**Related work landscape**  
Appendix A lists 55 recent surveys and reviews (2023‑2025) covering embodied AI, vision‑language‑action models, and foundation models for robotics.  Topics include embodied grasping, whole‑body control, multimodal large models, LLM integration for manipulation, motion planning, 3D perception, edge‑enabled federated foundations, neuroscience‑inspired agents, scaling laws, and systematic reviews of applications in autonomous driving, smart manufacturing, healthcare, and HRI.  Although the table reconstruction is incomplete, the bibliography demonstrates that the broader community is actively exploring many of the sub‑domains highlighted in the authors’ criteria catalogue, yet the quantitative analysis in this study shows that these explorations have not yet coalesced into models that satisfy the full set of industrial deployment requirements.

**Limitations of the evidence**  
All quantitative scores derive from an automated LLM‑based extraction pipeline applied to publication text; the authors acknowledge that the scores are context‑dependent estimates lacking confidence intervals, external validation, or direct performance measurements.  The reconstruction warnings (“結構未能可靠重建”) apply to several tables, limiting the ability to report fine‑grained numeric details beyond the aggregate scores explicitly stated.  Nevertheless, the reported maturity proportions, breadth–depth metrics, and expert‑LLM agreement rates constitute the only concrete evidence presented for the state of RFMs relative to the industrial criteria.

In sum, the study provides a comprehensive, criteria‑driven audit of 324 robot‑foundation models, revealing that while research has made modest progress on isolated capabilities such as adaptability and data efficiency, the field remains far from delivering integrated, deployment‑ready intelligence.  The authors’ roadmap—layered system design, edge‑aware benchmarking, and focused work on safety, HRI, real‑time operation, and cost‑effective integration—offers a clear direction for future work to bridge the identified gaps.
